name: messianic-prophecy
posts:
The most famous version of the messianic-prophecy argument is the one you should stop using.

You have heard the odds — one man, dozens of ancient prophecies.

Those probabilities are not measurements. They are guesses, multiplied.

Here is the one that holds.

Start with an honest rule.

In the New Testament, "fulfil" does not always mean "a prediction came true." Often it means "filled full" — an older pattern reaching its completion in Christ.

Pretending otherwise discredits the whole case.

So sort the prophecies.

Weak: anything a man could stage. Riding into Jerusalem on a donkey is the clearest example — the Gospels show Jesus deliberately arranging it.

Strong: what nobody can arrange. Birthplace. Lineage. The manner and timing of an execution under Roman law.

"But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah… from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel." (Micah 5:2)

A specific, falsifiable birthplace — one of the strongest data points in the case.

Nobody chooses the town, or the family, he is born into.

Then the verse that carries the most weight.

Isaiah 53:9 pairs a grave "with the wicked" and "with a rich man in his death."

Jesus was crucified between two criminals — and buried in the new tomb of a wealthy man.

A criminal's death. A rich man's grave. One verse.

And here is what we will not claim.

You will hear that Psalm 22 says "they pierced my hands and my feet," a thousand years early.

The standard Hebrew there reads "like a lion." The piercing reading is ancient — and genuinely contested.

So we rest the case on Isaiah 53:9.

Could the texts have been written after the fact, to fit him?

No. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran — all of chapter 53 included — is dated to roughly 125 BC. Well over a century before Jesus was born.

No one shaped Isaiah after the fact.

The strongest objection, stated fairly.

Jewish scholars answer that Isaiah's Servant is Israel — the nation is called God's servant a few chapters earlier.

That reading is sincere, and rooted in Isaiah's own words.

It deserves a real answer.

Within the song the Servant is stricken "for the transgression of my people" — distinguished from the people. And an ancient Jewish reading, the Targum on Isaiah 52:13, names "my servant the Messiah."

The referent is genuinely contested.

So what does the argument establish?

A single first-century figure fitting a constellation of expectations — birthplace, lineage, a rejected and suffering deliverer, a death and a burial — drawn from documents provably older than he was.

Not a proof. A portrait.

And it comes startlingly into focus on one face.

The full essay flags every disputed text as disputed — Isaiah 7:14, Psalm 22:16, Daniel 9, Isaiah 53's referent.

A serious case is one that can survive its own footnotes.
